extracted.intended_audience: students, legislators, constitutional designers, political theorists, and civic reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical guidance for how representative assemblies should be constituted and should behave: what powers they must retain, what functions they ought to perform or avoid, and institutional arrangements (commissions, ministers, committees) that produce good government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of representative government
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole people, or some numerous portion of them, exercise through deputies periodically elected by themselves the ultimate controlling power; this ultimate power must be possessed in all its completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The constitutional text need not explicitly give them every power; what matters is that representatives have final control in practice and can master government operations in the last resort. Representative government is defined by effective ultimate control, not by formal legal minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical supremacy must match real political power
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwritten constitutional maxims (positive political morality) only operate if they harmonize with the actual distribution of political strength; the body with the real active power should have practical predominance in the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Britain the crown's legal powers are nullified by constitutional morality because popular power preponderates. If legal provisions and unwritten maxims did not give supremacy to the element with real power, the Constitution would change. Stability depends on this alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies should control, not undertake all operations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a radical distinction between controlling the business of government and actually doing it: a representative assembly should control everything in the last resort but not attempt to perform all tasks itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large bodies cannot carry out many functions effectively (analogy: an army commander cannot fight in the ranks). The more a representative body delegates tasks it cannot do well, the better its control will be. Its province is to ensure tasks are well done by appropriate agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative bodies ought not to administer
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous representative bodies are generally unfit to administer public business or to dictate detailed administration; administration is usually better conducted under the responsibility of an individual or a small organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration requires organization, command, and specialized knowledge. Even small select boards are inferior to a competent single chief; joint-stock companies function better with a managing director. Assemblies as administrators lead to poor organization and weak individual responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly role in taxation: vote, do not originate estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of voting taxes belongs peculiarly to representative assemblies, but they should not prepare the estimates for taxation or appropriate revenues; money should be granted on the proposition of the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The maxim exists because moderation and careful allocation are expected when executive government is responsible for planning disbursements. Parliament's power is that of consent or refusal, not origination of tax proposals or detailed expenditure plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assemblies deciding detailed acts of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies attempting to decide on special acts of administration are likely to be inexperienced and ignorant of departmental rules and consequences, producing bad measures and appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative assemblies lack practical departmental knowledge; their judgments often ignore important traditions or precautions. When interested motives intervene, even a few biased members can mislead the body, leading to jobbery and corruption. Assemblies rarely suffer personal consequences for such votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments require individual responsibility, not collective nomination
rubrics_metrics.description: Nomination to public employments imperatively requires strong individual responsibility because assemblies are weak at judging special qualifications and are prone to partisan or unqualified choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers and heads of offices, who bear individual responsibility, are better placed to appoint fit persons. Assemblies tend to appoint on reputation, popularity, or party advantage rather than true qualifications; this produces poor appointments and patronage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament should not directly nominate cabinets
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient for Parliament to decide, virtually, the choice of a prime minister or which party supplies the executive; actual nomination and appointment should remain the executive's or follow arrangements fitting the constitution's form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the British practice Parliament recognizes the party to furnish the executive; the crown appoints leaders in conformity with parliamentary wishes. In republics alternative arrangements (independent election of executive or naming a prime minister responsible for choices) are necessary to preserve responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative work requires few, expert drafters
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmaking needs experienced, exercised, and specially trained minds; numerous assemblies are poorly suited to frame laws, which should be prepared by a small committee of very few persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every provision of law must be accurately framed with long-sighted perception of effects on other provisions and consistency with existing laws. Clause-by-clause voting in a miscellaneous assembly produces incoherence; a small expert body can produce coherent legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a permanent Legislative Commission (Commission of Codification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A permanent, small Commission of Legislation should be entrusted with drafting and codifying laws; Parliament would pass or reject measures but not alter them in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioners should prepare bills, respond to Parliament's instructions, and remain without power to enact. Practical proposals: appointment by crown, five-year terms, removal by address for misconduct or refusal, reappointment subject to evaluation. Parliament may refer subjects or drafts to the commission and remit measures for reconsideration; final enactment remains with Parliament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tinkering bills in a miscellaneous assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing the House to amend bills clause by clause leads to omission of essential clauses, insertion of incongruous provisions to placate private interests, and the foisting of ill-considered clauses by members with inadequate knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-prepared bills by commissions or select bodies are mangled by committee-of-the-whole procedures and time constraints. Referring bills to select committees or a legislative commission reduces waste of time and poor amendments; reliance on committee-of-the-whole is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly's proper functions: publicity, scrutiny, and control
rubrics_metrics.description: The representative assembly's proper office is to watch and control the government: expose its acts to publicity, compel full exposition and justification, censure if condemnable, and expel or replace men who abuse their trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This surveillance and power to enforce accountability constitute ample security for liberty. The assembly should act as the nation's Committee of Grievances and ensure transparent justification of government acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assembly as forum for national opinion and deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should serve as the nation's Congress of Opinions, an arena where every section and eminent individual can have views expressed and tested in adversarial debate, enabling the nation's opinions to manifest and marshal support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such debate helps statesmen identify growing or declining elements of opinion and shape measures accordingly. 'Talking' is a valuable function when it does not replace doing; it enables minority opinions to be heard and majority sentiment to manifest itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure that those who do the work are properly selected and accountable
rubrics_metrics.description: The assembly's duty is to determine to whom or to what sort of people particular governmental tasks should be confided and to give or withhold national sanction to their performance, rather than to perform the tasks themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where assemblies lack competence, they should arrange for experts or responsible individuals to perform tasks and then monitor and sanction them. The assembly's competency is in selecting and checking, not in executing specialized functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unwritten constitutional rules should limit exercise of legal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutional morality—unwritten maxims and political habits—serves to nullify or restrain legal powers that could otherwise be used destructively (e.g., royal veto or appointment powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These norms maintain stability only if they reflect real political strength; they are precautions the ruling power allows against its own errors. Reliance on these unwritten rules is part of practical constitutional functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware tendency of assemblies to overreach when strong
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative bodies, as they gain stronger power, have a practical tendency to interfere increasingly in administrative detail and legislation, posing a danger to the proper balance of functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This overreach is driven by temptation to use strength excessively and may jeopardize the future effectiveness of representative governments. Institutional safeguards and norms are needed to prevent encroachment into functions better handled by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation is the distinctive competence of assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: The unique strength of a large deliberative body is its capacity for hearing and considering many conflicting opinions; deliberation is what a body can do better than any single individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies should concentrate on deliberative tasks—public debate, airing sectional grievances, and testing opinions—while delegating execution to individuals or small bodies with specialized knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws must be coherent with existing legal framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Every provision of a law requires accurate framing and long-sighted perception of its effects on all other provisions so that laws fit into a consistent whole with existing laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because legislation interacts with the whole body of law, hasty clause-by-clause amendments by an unskilled assembly create chaos. This is a principal reason for relying on expert drafters or a codifying commission.
